title: Boss build: Mad Libs
hook: Build a silly story game that uses everything from week 1.

warmup.q: Someone types 6 into an `input`. What kind of value do you get?
warmup.explain: `input` always gives text. Use `int()` or `float()` to convert.
The curly brackets are swapped for the stored value.

warmup.q: Python shows an error. What is the first thing to do?
warmup.explain: The error names the line. Look there first.

why.heading: Boss day
why.text:
Every Friday you build a small game or tool out of the week's pieces. Today: **Mad Libs**. The program asks for words without telling you the story, then drops your words into a silly story.

You already know everything needed: `input`, variables, `int`, f-strings.

why.heading: Plan before typing
why.text:
Good programmers plan first. For today:

1. Ask for the words.
2. Convert any numbers.
3. Print the story.

Ask first, tell last. Your three tasks add one piece each, and task 3 is the finished game.

why.heading: Comments
why.text:
A line starting with `#` is a **comment**. Python ignores it completely. It is a note for the human reading the code, including you next week.

`# ask for the words`

You can also put one at the end of a line: `print(x)  # shows x`.

why.heading: Why comments help
why.text:
By Friday, code you wrote on Monday looks like a stranger wrote it. Comments say what a step is for.

They also switch lines off while testing: put `#` in front of a line and Python skips it. Take the `#` off to bring it back.

why.heading: Build in small steps
why.text: Run after every small step. If step 1 works and step 2 breaks, you know the bug is in step 2. This is how real programs get built: small, working, then a bit more.

watch.intro: Tap Run. A tiny Mad Libs with a comment above it. The answer (mango) is typed for you.
watch.code:
# Ask for a fruit, then use it
word = input("A fruit? ")
print(f"I love {word}!")  # this comment is at the end of a line
explain: The first line is a comment. Python skips it.
The comment at the end of the last line is skipped too.
Only the two real lines do any work.
watch.break_it: Break it on purpose: delete the `#` at the start of line 1 so it reads `Ask for a fruit, then use it` and tap Run. You get `SyntaxError: invalid syntax`. Without the `#`, Python tries to read your note as code. Put the `#` back.

tasks.title: Step 1: the opening
tasks.task:
Add a comment line (starting with `#`) that says what the program is. Then ask for an animal and a place and print the first line of the story. For `lion` and `Cape Town`:

`Animal? lion`
`Place? Cape Town`
`The lion ran to Cape Town.`
tasks.solution:
# Mad Libs step 1
animal = input("Animal? ")
place = input("Place? ")
print(f"The {animal} ran to {place}.")
hints: Ask for the place the same way as the animal. The question is Place? with a space after it.
Add a line such as # Mad Libs step 1 at the top, and print with an f-string.

tests.expect:
Animal? lion
Place? Cape Town
The lion ran to Cape Town.

Animal? gecko
Place? Durban
The gecko ran to Durban.

tasks.title: Step 2: add a number
tasks.task:
Two more questions: `Adjective?` and then `Number?` (a whole number). The story gets an adjective and a second line that doubles the number. For `lion`, `Cape Town`, `tiny`, `3`:

`The tiny lion ran to Cape Town.`
`It did 3 laps, then 6 more.`
tasks.starter:
# Step 2
animal = input("Animal? ")
place = input("Place? ")
# ask Adjective? and Number? (convert the number)
# print the two story lines
tasks.solution:
# Step 2
animal = input("Animal? ")
place = input("Place? ")
adj = input("Adjective? ")
n = int(input("Number? "))
print(f"The {adj} {animal} ran to {place}.")
print(f"It did {n} laps, then {n * 2} more.")
hints: Ask for the adjective, then the number, in that order, after the place.
The number must be an int, so you can do n * 2.

tests.expect:
Animal? lion
Place? Cape Town
Adjective? tiny
Number? 3
The tiny lion ran to Cape Town.
It did 3 laps, then 6 more.

Animal? gecko
Place? Durban
Adjective? angry
Number? 10
The angry gecko ran to Durban.
It did 10 laps, then 20 more.

tasks.title: Step 3: Set Mad Libs
tasks.task:
The finished game, film set edition. Print the banner first, ask four questions (`Name?`, `Job?`, `Item?`, `Takes?` where takes is a whole number), then print a three line story. Overtime is R500 per take. For `Zola`, `gaffer`, `lamp`, `4`:

`=== SET MAD LIBS ===`
`Name? Zola`
`Job? gaffer`
`Item? lamp`
`Takes? 4`
`Zola the gaffer arrived with a giant lamp.`
`It took 4 takes to get the shot.`
`Overtime cost R2000. Wrap!`
tasks.starter:
# Set Mad Libs: the finished game
# 1. print the banner
# 2. ask the four questions
# 3. print the story
tasks.solution:
# Set Mad Libs
print("=== SET MAD LIBS ===")
name = input("Name? ")
job = input("Job? ")
item = input("Item? ")
takes = int(input("Takes? "))
print(f"{name} the {job} arrived with a giant {item}.")
print(f"It took {takes} takes to get the shot.")
print(f"Overtime cost R{takes * 500}. Wrap!")
hints: Start with print("=== SET MAD LIBS ==="), then four input lines. Convert only Takes.
takes = int(input("Takes? ")) lets you do takes * 500 later.
The last line is print(f"Overtime cost R{takes * 500}. Wrap!")

tests.expect:
=== SET MAD LIBS ===
Name? Zola
Job? gaffer
Item? lamp
Takes? 4
Zola the gaffer arrived with a giant lamp.
It took 4 takes to get the shot.
Overtime cost R2000. Wrap!

=== SET MAD LIBS ===
Name? Ayanda
Job? boom op
Item? fish
Takes? 7
Ayanda the boom op arrived with a giant fish.
It took 7 takes to get the shot.
Overtime cost R3500. Wrap!

recap: A `#` comment is a note for humans. Python ignores it.
Build in small steps and run after each one.
You can now make a program that talks, asks, calculates and tells a story. That is week 1 done.

words.meaning: A note starting with # that Python ignores.
Python cannot read the line as code at all.
A Friday project that uses the whole week.
